title: Cerebral Lobes Atlas
subtitle: Compare frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital and insular territories
altText: Interactive chalkboard-style anatomical atlas of Cerebral Lobes with labelled regions and pathway relationships.
learningObjectives: Identify the five major cerebral lobes in lateral and medial views.
Compare characteristic functions without reducing cognition to one lobe.
Relate cortical territories to blood supply and common lesion presentations.

sections.explainSimply: The cerebral cortex is divided into broad lobes that specialise in different kinds of information while continuously working together.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Lobe labels are useful orientation tools, but psychological functions arise from distributed networks that cross anatomical boundaries.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital and insular cortices contain multiple cytoarchitectonic and connectional territories. Clinical interpretation therefore depends on lesion location, laterality, white-matter disconnection and network compensation rather than lobe name alone.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of the lobes as districts in one city: each has characteristic services, but roads, utilities and people constantly cross district borders.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Lobe-level orientation helps psychologists connect behavioural change with plausible neural systems while avoiding crude localisation claims.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Treating one lobe as the sole home of a complex function can produce inaccurate formulation and overconfident lesion inference.
sections.clinicalPearl: Use lobes to orient; use networks, tracts and task demands to explain.
sections.practicalExample: A left posterior temporal lesion may disrupt language comprehension, but the person’s functional profile also depends on auditory processing, semantic networks and interhemispheric support.
sections.limitationsCautions: Individual variation is substantial. A lobe map cannot diagnose impairment or predict outcome without examination, imaging and functional assessment.

anatomy.label: Frontal lobe
anatomy.function: Executive control, action selection, motor planning and social regulation
anatomy.inputs: Thalamic, limbic, sensory-association and contralateral cortical input
anatomy.outputs: Motor, striatal, thalamic, limbic and association-cortex outputs
anatomy.connections: Thalamic, limbic, sensory-association and contralateral cortical input; projects via Motor, striatal, thalamic, limbic and association-cortex outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Disinhibition, apathy, dysexecutive syndromes, motor deficits
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess frontal lobe in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Parietal lobe
anatomy.function: Multisensory integration, body representation, spatial attention and skilled action
anatomy.inputs: Somatosensory, visual, auditory and thalamic input
anatomy.outputs: Premotor, frontal, temporal and subcortical outputs
anatomy.connections: Somatosensory, visual, auditory and thalamic input; projects via Premotor, frontal, temporal and subcortical outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Neglect, apraxia, dyscalculia, somatosensory integration deficits
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess parietal lobe in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Temporal lobe
anatomy.function: Auditory analysis, semantic memory, object recognition and episodic-memory interfaces
anatomy.inputs: Auditory, visual, limbic and association-cortex input
anatomy.outputs: Frontal, parietal, limbic and subcortical outputs
anatomy.connections: Auditory, visual, limbic and association-cortex input; projects via Frontal, parietal, limbic and subcortical outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Aphasia, memory impairment, agnosia, altered emotion processing
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess temporal lobe in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Occipital lobe
anatomy.inputs: Thalamic visual input through the lateral geniculate nucleus
anatomy.connections: Thalamic visual input through the lateral geniculate nucleus; projects via Dorsal and ventral visual-stream outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Visual field loss, cortical blindness, visual perceptual deficits
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess occipital lobe in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

anatomy.label: Insula
anatomy.function: Interoception, salience, taste and integration of bodily state with emotion
anatomy.inputs: Visceral, somatosensory, limbic and thalamic input
anatomy.outputs: Cingulate, frontal, temporal, autonomic and subcortical outputs
anatomy.connections: Visceral, somatosensory, limbic and thalamic input; projects via Cingulate, frontal, temporal, autonomic and subcortical outputs.
anatomy.associatedDisorders: Altered interoception, taste disturbance, salience dysregulation
anatomy.clinicalSignificance: Assess insula in the context of lesion location, laterality, tract involvement and functional change.

quiz.question: Why do connections matter clinically?
options: Symptoms may reflect disconnection and downstream network effects.
quiz.rationale: Distributed cognitive functions depend on connected pathways.

quiz.question: What should an atlas not be used for?
options: Making a diagnosis from one structure alone.
quiz.rationale: An atlas is an educational and hypothesis-support tool, not a standalone diagnostic instrument.
